new_statements.quote: The syllable is defined as the rank whose units have a structure in terms of phonemes and which functions in the rhythm group. The rhythm group consists of one to three syllables; only the last is stressed. The bulk of the language corpus consists of rhythm groups with only one syllable. The focus of this study is therefore on the more complex stressed syllable. The core of the stressed syllable includes a consonantal margin, a vocalic nucleus and a tonal prosody.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tone language (four level tones plus three contour sequences, and a ballistic/controlled syllable contrast). The phonological word ('rhythm group') is one to three syllables long and stress falls on its last syllable; any preceding syllables are unstressed pretonic syllables with reduced segmental and tonal inventories. Most words are monosyllabic. Corroborated independently by Lewis & Rensch 1971 ms. sec.7: the core of the phonological word is the stressed syllable, optionally preceded by 'one or rarely two pretonic syllables'; ballistic accent occurs only in the stressed syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: None. (Spanish loans such as /ka4hwi1/ 'cow', /pi lai/ 'Felipe' are cited with the same pretonic + stressed-final shape.) The contrastive 'ballistic stress/accent' marked with an acute is a syllable-type feature of the stressed syllable, not a competing stress position.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is Thelin's 'rhythm group' = Lewis & Rensch's 'phonological word' (root syllable plus up to two prefixal/pretonic syllables); statements are about word-level forms in isolation and in text, not phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Both primary sources describe the Chinantec of San Juan Bautista Tlacoatzintepec (Cuicatlan district, Oaxaca) = Glottolog tlac1239 / ISO ctl exactly; Thelin notes the same variety is spoken in surrounding hamlets and by migrants in Chiltepec, with minor phonological differences among the town's three barrios. No dialect mismatch.

sources.note: p.1 Introduction: 'The rhythm group consists of one to three syllables; only the last is stressed. The bulk of the language corpus consists of rhythm groups with only one syllable.' Sec.3 'The prosody' (pp.5-6): syllables are ballistic (acute accent) or controlled; four level tones (1 very high... 4 low) plus sequences 12, 34, 42; 'two tones or one tone and ballistic stress' in the maximal syllable; /r/ is an affricate in stressed syllables, a flap in unstressed syllables (p.2).

sources.citation: Lewis, Mabel et al. 2015 [files of the 3rd ed.; 4th ed. 2020 = SIL archives entry 85886]. Aprendamos a leer y escribir en el idioma chinanteco (chinanteco de Tlacoatzintepec). Oaxaca: Instituto Linguistico de Verano. ca. 306 pp. Stated in its preface to be the revised edition of Lewis 1988 'Leyendo y escribiendo el idioma chinanteco'.
sources.note: Transition primer. Leccion 1 p.7: four basic tones marked with orthographic signs; Leccion 13 p.87: 'En chinanteco las palabras que se pronuncian con mas fuerza se escriben con acento' (the written acute = ballistic accent, contrastive, e.g. jan 'pluma' vs jan-with-accent 'espuma'). Nothing on which syllable of a polysyllable is stressed.
